questions.stem: At Xerxes' accession, the Persian Empire stretched from:
options: Mesopotamia in the west to the Yellow River valley of China in the east
the Aegean and Egypt in the west to the Indus valley in the east
the Atlantic coast of Spain in the west to the Caspian Sea in the east
the Black Sea in the north to the southern tip of Arabia only
questions.explanation: The Achaemenid Empire ruled Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Mesopotamia, Iran, Central Asia and the Indus region. It never reached Spain or China.

questions.stem: The Persian king's title 'King of Kings' expressed the idea that he:
options: shared his throne equally with the kings of Egypt and Babylon as allies
ruled over many lands and peoples, each with its own rulers and customs
was elected by the kings of the subject peoples at a council in Babylon
was the son of a god and was worshipped as a god in his own lifetime
questions.explanation: Royal inscriptions call the king King of Kings and king of lands of many peoples. Achaemenid kings ruled by the favour of Ahura Mazda but were not worshipped as gods in Persia.

questions.stem: Royal reliefs at Persepolis show the king enthroned, with delegations of subject peoples bringing gifts. What image of kingship did they project?
options: A priest-king who spent most of his life in prayer in the temples
An ordered empire of willing peoples united under the king's rule
A warrior king shown killing his enemies and burning their cities
A king who shared power equally with a council of elected nobles
questions.explanation: Persepolis art shows peaceful harmony: subject peoples in their own dress bring gifts, and no battle scenes appear. This contrasts with Assyrian palace reliefs, which often show violent conquest.

questions.stem: Xerxes was the son of:
options: Cambyses II and his sister-wife, Roxane of Persia
Artaxerxes I and the Babylonian princess, Amestris
Darius I and Atossa, a daughter of Cyrus the Great
Cyrus the Great and his Median queen, Cassandane
questions.explanation: Xerxes' mother, Atossa, was a daughter of Cyrus, the founder of the empire. Through her, Xerxes joined Darius's line to Cyrus's, which strengthened his claim.

questions.stem: Herodotus says that Xerxes was chosen as heir over his older half-brother Artobazanes. Why, according to Herodotus, did Xerxes have the stronger claim?
options: He was born after Darius became king and his mother was a daughter of Cyrus
He had won a great victory over the Scythians while his brother was a child
The Magi chose him after reading the signs in the sacred fire at Pasargadae
His brother had rebelled against Darius and had been exiled to Egypt
questions.explanation: Herodotus reports that Xerxes was born to Atossa after Darius took the throne, while Artobazanes was born before it to a commoner wife. He adds that the exiled Spartan king Demaratus advised this argument.

questions.stem: An inscription of Xerxes at Persepolis states that Darius made him 'the greatest after himself' although Darius had other sons. What does this source suggest?
options: Xerxes admitted that he had seized the throne by force from his brothers
Darius had shared the throne equally with all his sons in his lifetime
Xerxes was the eldest of Darius's sons and so had an automatic right
Xerxes wished to show that his succession was his father's own choice
questions.explanation: The text answers any doubt about his claim by stressing Darius's choice. It also concedes that there were other sons, so primogeniture alone did not decide the succession.

questions.stem: Xerxes became king in:
options: 486 BCE
490 BCE
480 BCE
465 BCE
questions.explanation: Darius I died in late 486 BCE and Xerxes succeeded him. 490 BCE was the year of Marathon, 480 BCE the invasion of Greece, and 465 BCE the year of Xerxes' death.

questions.stem: Herodotus says Xerxes' elite infantry of 10,000, the Immortals, were so called because:
options: they never fought in battle and so none of them had ever been killed by an enemy
any man who died or fell ill was at once replaced, keeping the unit at full strength
they had all survived wounds in battle and were believed to be protected by the gods
they were the sons of gods, according to the Persian priests who chose them as boys
questions.explanation: Herodotus explains that the number never fell below 10,000 because each loss was filled at once. The Immortals fought at Thermopylae, so they did see battle.

questions.stem: The Persian Empire under Xerxes was divided into provinces governed by:
options: hereditary kings who paid no tribute and owed the king no service
satraps, appointed by the king and often drawn from Persian nobles
elected councils of citizens who voted on the taxes owed each year
the priests of the local temples, who collected tribute for the king
questions.explanation: Satraps ran their provinces, collected tribute and kept order, while royal officials and the king's family ties helped keep them loyal.

questions.stem: The Royal Road ran from Sardis to Susa, with stations where messengers changed horses. Why was it important to Xerxes' government?
options: It linked Persia to India so that the Indus could be added later
It carried royal messages and officials quickly across the empire
It was the only road along which the army was permitted to travel
It allowed merchants to avoid paying any tolls or royal taxes at all
questions.explanation: Herodotus admired the speed of the relay messengers. The road helped the king and his officials control distant satrapies such as Lydia.

questions.stem: Early in his reign, Xerxes put down a revolt in Egypt and appointed as satrap:
options: his general Mardonius
the eunuch Aspamitres
his full brother Achaemenes
the Spartan exile Demaratus
questions.explanation: Egypt revolted at the end of Darius's reign and was subdued by about 484 BCE. Xerxes then made his brother Achaemenes satrap, keeping a vital province in the family.

questions.stem: Babylon revolted against Xerxes twice, under Bel-shimanni and later under Shamash-eriba. What was a likely result of the second revolt?
options: Babylon became independent and was never again ruled by the Persians
Xerxes moved his capital from Persepolis to Babylon to watch the city
The Babylonians were all deported to Persia and the city was left empty
Tighter Persian control of Babylon, though how harsh it was is debated
questions.explanation: After the revolts, Babylonian records show changes in leading families and administration. Greek stories that Xerxes destroyed temples or removed Marduk's statue are disputed by modern historians.

questions.stem: Greek writers claimed that Xerxes destroyed the temple of Marduk in Babylon. Many modern historians doubt this mainly because:
options: Babylonian texts say Xerxes worshipped Marduk as his only true god
Herodotus admits he invented the story to entertain his audience
The temple had been destroyed by the Assyrians long before Xerxes was born
Babylonian sources show the cult and temple continuing after his reign
questions.explanation: Cuneiform texts show the temple and its cult still functioning, so a total destruction is unlikely. The Greek story may exaggerate a punishment of the rebel city or confuse different events.

questions.stem: Xerxes' inscriptions say that he ruled by the favour of:
options: Ahura Mazda
Marduk
Amun-Ra
Zeus
questions.explanation: Achaemenid kings credited their power to Ahura Mazda, the great god of the Persians. Marduk was the god of Babylon and Amun-Ra the chief god of Egypt.

questions.stem: In the 'Daiva inscription', Xerxes states that he destroyed a sanctuary of the daivas, false gods, in a land that had rebelled, and established the worship of Ahura Mazda there. Why is this source debated?
options: It does not name the land, so historians cannot link it to a known revolt
It was written in Greek, a language Persian kings never used in inscriptions
It was found at Athens, so it may describe the burning of the Acropolis
It contradicts Herodotus, who says Xerxes respected every god of Greece
questions.explanation: The inscription is general and leaves the land unnamed. Some link it to Egypt or Babylon, others see it as a statement of royal ideals, so it cannot prove a policy of religious persecution.

questions.stem: Under the Achaemenids, the Magi were:
options: officers of the Immortals who guarded the king on campaigns abroad
scribes who wrote royal letters in Aramaic to the distant satrapies
priests who performed rituals, including those connected with fire
royal judges who heard appeals from the satrapies in the king's name
questions.explanation: Herodotus and Persian administrative tablets show the Magi as ritual specialists. Fire held a central place in Persian worship.

questions.stem: Herodotus describes Xerxes burning the temples on the Athenian Acropolis in 480 BCE, but also offering sacrifice to Athena at Troy and ordering Athenian exiles to sacrifice on the Acropolis. What do these accounts suggest?
options: His treatment of temples depended on politics, not hostility to all foreign gods
He was a religious fanatic who tried to force all Greeks to worship Ahura Mazda
He was a secret worshipper of the Greek gods who had turned against Persia
Herodotus could not decide which gods Xerxes worshipped and guessed at them
questions.explanation: Burning Athens' temples punished the city, including for the burning of Sardis in the Ionian Revolt, while other acts honoured local gods. Persian kings generally tolerated subject peoples' cults.

questions.stem: Which building at Persepolis did Xerxes build, with colossal winged bulls at its doors?
options: The Hanging Gardens
The Gate of All Nations
The Ishtar Gate
The Parthenon
questions.explanation: Xerxes' inscription on the Gate of All Nations says he built it. The Ishtar Gate and the gardens belong to Babylon, and the Parthenon to Athens.

questions.stem: At Persepolis, Xerxes completed the Apadana begun by Darius and began the Hall of a Hundred Columns. What does this building program suggest about his reign?
options: He was so short of money after Greece that all building stopped there
He built only fortifications, since he feared a Greek attack on Persia
He continued his father's plans and displayed the wealth of the empire
He abandoned his father's capital and built a new one in Babylon instead
questions.explanation: Inscriptions credit Xerxes with major works at Persepolis, finishing his father's projects and adding his own. Building continued after 480 BCE, so the Greek defeat did not ruin the empire.

questions.stem: The Persepolis Treasury and Fortification tablets record payments to workers in rations and silver. What do they show about building at Persepolis?
options: Only enslaved Greek prisoners of war built the palaces at Persepolis
The palaces were built by the army during the winters between wars
Persian nobles paid for the building out of their own estates alone
Paid workers from many lands, including women, built the complex
questions.explanation: The tablets record skilled and unskilled workers from across the empire receiving rations and wages, with women among them, some receiving extra rations after giving birth.

questions.stem: To prepare for the invasion of Greece, Xerxes ordered:
options: a road built from Egypt across Libya so that his army could attack from Africa
a canal cut across the Athos peninsula and bridges built over the Hellespont
a wall built across the Isthmus of Corinth to stop the Spartans moving north
a fleet built on the Black Sea so that it could sail around Greece from the west
questions.explanation: The canal let the fleet avoid the stormy cape where Darius's fleet had been wrecked in 492 BCE, and boat bridges carried the army from Asia to Europe.

questions.stem: Herodotus says that when a storm destroyed the first Hellespont bridges, Xerxes had the water given three hundred lashes. How should a historian use this story?
options: As Herodotus's portrait of a proud, impious king, not as plain fact
As proof that Xerxes was insane, since no sane ruler would ever do such a thing
As a Persian ritual, since Persian texts describe it in detail
As a later Roman addition that Herodotus never actually wrote
questions.explanation: The story fits Herodotus's theme of hubris before a fall. It may reflect a real act or a Greek misreading of a ritual, but it cannot be taken at face value.

questions.stem: After the defeat at Salamis in 480 BCE, Xerxes:
options: returned to Asia and left Mardonius with an army in Greece
stayed on in Athens until the Greeks forced him to surrender
sailed home with his whole army and never fought again
made peace with Sparta and divided Greece between them
questions.explanation: Xerxes went back to Sardis, leaving Mardonius to continue the war on land. Mardonius was defeated and killed at Plataea in 479 BCE.

questions.stem: In 479 BCE the Persians lost both the Battle of Plataea on land and the Battle of Mycale in Ionia. What was the main consequence of Mycale?
options: Xerxes was overthrown and replaced by his brother as King of Kings
Athens captured Sardis and began the conquest of Anatolia for itself
The Ionian Greek cities could revolt again, and Persia lost the Aegean
Persia lost Egypt, which used the defeat to declare its own independence
questions.explanation: The destruction of the Persian fleet at Mycale opened the way for the Ionians to break away and for the Delian League to fight on in the Aegean. The empire itself remained intact.

questions.stem: Herodotus presents the invasion of Greece as a great disaster for Xerxes. Many modern historians argue instead that:
options: the defeat caused the Persian Empire to collapse within a few years
Greece was a frontier setback for an empire that stayed powerful long after
the invasion was a complete success, since Xerxes conquered all of mainland Greece
Xerxes never meant to invade and only sent a small force to punish Athens
questions.explanation: Xerxes burnt Athens, as he had set out to punish it, and the empire kept its vast eastern lands for another 150 years. From Persia's point of view, Greece was on the edge of the empire.

questions.stem: Artemisia, who commanded ships in Xerxes' fleet at Salamis, was:
options: a priestess of Athena from Athens
the ruler of Halicarnassus in Caria
a Spartan queen held as a hostage
Xerxes' sister and chief wife
questions.explanation: Artemisia ruled Halicarnassus, Herodotus's own city, as a Persian subject. Herodotus says she advised Xerxes not to fight at sea at Salamis.

questions.stem: Herodotus has the exiled Spartan king Demaratus warn Xerxes that the Spartans fear their law more than his subjects fear him. What is the purpose of these conversations in Herodotus?
options: To contrast free Greeks under law with subjects under a single ruler
To record Demaratus's actual words, which were kept in Persian archives
To show that Demaratus secretly planned to betray Xerxes to the Greeks
To prove that Spartans were weaker in battle than the Persian Immortals
questions.explanation: The dialogues dramatise a central Greek theme of the Histories. They are literary creations, though Demaratus really did live at the Persian court.

questions.stem: Mardonius, Xerxes' cousin and brother-in-law, is presented by Herodotus as:
options: the eunuch who later murdered Xerxes in his bedroom
the leading advocate of the invasion of Greece
the general who opposed the invasion from the start
the satrap of Egypt who refused to send any ships
questions.explanation: Herodotus says Mardonius urged Xerxes to punish Athens and expand into Europe, while Xerxes' uncle Artabanus warned against it. Mardonius died at Plataea.

questions.stem: Xerxes was murdered in 465 BCE by:
options: Artabanus, the commander of the royal guard
Pausanias, the Spartan regent, in revenge for Plataea
his brother Achaemenes, the satrap of Egypt
Themistocles, the Athenian who fled to his court
questions.explanation: Greek sources say Artabanus, head of the bodyguard, killed Xerxes in a palace plot. His son Artaxerxes I succeeded after Artabanus was in turn killed.

questions.stem: What does Xerxes' murder and the struggle that followed suggest about Achaemenid kingship?
options: Each king named a Greek adviser to choose the heir after his death
The empire was ruled by a council for years until a king came of age
Succession was not fixed, and court factions could decide who ruled
Kings were elected by the army, so a new king was chosen peacefully
questions.explanation: Several Achaemenid kings came to the throne after murders or disputes. Xerxes' death and the killing of his son Darius show how dangerous court politics could be.

questions.stem: Aeschylus' tragedy The Persians, performed in Athens in 472 BCE, is significant because it:
options: contains the full text of Xerxes' royal decrees translated into the Greek language
was banned in Athens because it praised Xerxes as a wise and successful king
is the earliest surviving Greek work about Xerxes, written within a decade of Salamis
was written by a Persian noble who had fought for Xerxes in the Greek campaign
questions.explanation: Aeschylus fought against the Persians and staged the defeat from the Persian court's point of view. The play shows Xerxes lamenting his folly, an Athenian view of Persian pride.

questions.stem: Why is Herodotus both valuable and problematic as a source for Xerxes?
options: He lived at Xerxes' court for years, but could not read any Greek sources at all
He used the Persian royal archives, but wrote three centuries after the war
He was an eyewitness at Salamis, but wrote his account only in old Persian
He gathered detailed accounts soon after, but wrote for Greeks with a moral theme
questions.explanation: Herodotus, born in Persian-ruled Halicarnassus, collected oral traditions within a generation or two of the war. His work explores Greek freedom against Persian monarchy and the punishment of pride.

questions.stem: Persian royal inscriptions and administrative tablets about Xerxes differ from Greek sources mainly because they:
options: describe the Greek war in great detail and admit the defeat at Salamis
were written by Greek scribes who wanted to flatter the Persian king
focus on Xerxes' private life and his quarrels with his wives and sons
present the official royal view and say little about the war with Greece
questions.explanation: Persian sources record building, piety, administration and payments. They are silent on the Greek campaign, so the narrative depends on Greek writers.

questions.stem: The Persian Masistes, Xerxes' brother, appears in Herodotus in a story of harem intrigue and cruelty at the end of the Histories. A historian evaluating Herodotus's picture of Xerxes would note that:
options: Persian sources confirm every detail of the story, so it must be accurate
the story is told by Aeschylus, so Herodotus must have copied it from him
the story concerns Darius, not Xerxes, so it tells us nothing about his reign
Greek tales of court scandal echo stereotypes of Persian luxury and despotism
questions.explanation: Stories of a weak king ruled by the harem became a stock image in later Greek writing. Historians weigh them carefully, since Persian sources give no such picture.

questions.stem: Modern scholars such as Pierre Briant and Heleen Sancisi-Weerdenburg argued that Xerxes' reputation as a cruel, decadent failure:
options: rested on Egyptian papyri that recorded his conquest of the Nile valley
came largely from Greek sources and should be tested against Persian evidence
was fully confirmed by Persian inscriptions that criticised his whole reign
was invented by twentieth-century historians with no basis in ancient texts
questions.explanation: These historians stressed Persian sources and archaeology, which show a king who ruled a stable empire for twenty years and built on a grand scale.

questions.stem: Which judgement of Xerxes' reign is best supported by the evidence?
options: He kept the empire intact and built on a large scale, despite failure in Greece
He lost most of the empire, including Egypt and Babylon, after Salamis
He was a weak ruler who never left his palace and let the satraps rule as they wished
He made Persia a Greek-style state by adopting Athenian democratic ideas
questions.explanation: Xerxes put down revolts in Egypt and Babylon, completed major buildings at Persepolis and passed on an intact empire. His failure in Greece mattered greatly to Greeks but less to Persia.

questions.stem: Historians studying Xerxes rely heavily on archaeology at Persepolis. What is its main value?
options: It shows his building and royal image in his own terms, unlike the Greek texts
It contains a full written narrative of his campaigns against the Greeks year by year
It proves that the city was destroyed by Xerxes at the end of his reign
It records the names of every soldier who fought at Thermopylae for him
questions.explanation: Inscriptions, reliefs and tablets from Persepolis show the king as Persians presented him. The city was burnt later, by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE.
